title: Supreme Court Seeks Public Notice So All 51 War Victims' Families Can Claim Compensation
excerpt: The court asked the External Affairs Ministry to consider a public notice inviting every bereaved family to claim, after the government said 51 Indians died, 139 were discharged and 77 remain untraced in the Russia-Ukraine war.
body:
• The Supreme Court on Wednesday asked the Ministry of External Affairs to consider a public notice inviting families of all 51 Indians who died fighting in the Russia-Ukraine war to seek assistance and compensation.
  • The government told the court 267 Indians joined the Russian armed forces: 51 died, 139 were discharged, and 77 remain untraced, including seven Russia has confirmed as missing.
  • Russia has processed six compensation claims so far — five settled fully and one partially — and the court sought a fresh status report specifying what those six families were paid.
  • Reader utility: families in Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh are entitled to free legal aid from their District Legal Services Authorities for compensation claims, DNA tests and related formalities.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday said the right to seek compensation must be enforced and asked the Ministry of External Affairs to consider issuing a public notice inviting the families of Indians who died while fighting in the Russia-Ukraine war to seek assistance and compensation, according to India Today reporting republished by News89. A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi was hearing a plea concerning Indian nationals allegedly duped by agents and recruited into the Russian military.

The new step is reach. The ministry told the bench it has been contacting affected families individually. A public notice would extend the compensation right, in the court's words, to the families of all 51 people who died — including families the government has not yet traced or who do not know a claim is available to them.

The numbers the government placed on record

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre, told the court about 267 Indians had joined the Russian armed forces. Of them, 51 had died and 139 had been discharged from military service. The Indian embassy in Russia was trying to trace 77 recruits, including seven whom Russian authorities had confirmed as missing.

On compensation, Bhati said the Russian government had processed six claims: five settled fully and one partially. The court asked the ministry to file a fresh status report specifying the compensation paid by the Russian government to those six families. It also reviewed efforts to identify and repatriate mortal remains, secure compensation and help families complete legal and administrative formalities, and it noted the difficulties involved — delays in DNA-based identification, and the process of obtaining compensation from Russia.

The bench asked the District Legal Services Authorities of Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh to comply with its earlier direction to provide free legal aid, covering submission of claims, DNA tests and other formalities. The court also examined a separate case, that of Sikandar Singh, sentenced to eight years in prison in Russia, and whether a transfer to an Indian prison could be explored; Bhati said he would first have to withdraw his appeal in Russia.

How the case reached this point

On July 31, the court had already directed the Centre to appoint a nodal officer in the ministry to coordinate with families, arrange DNA profiling of mortal remains before bodies are handed over, supply families a complete procedure for filing compensation claims with the Russian authorities through the MEA, and provide free legal aid, LiveLaw reported in the case Divya v. Union of India. That order also made clear that a pending compensation claim must not delay handing over mortal remains or cremation.

The underlying allegations are that men who travelled to Russia in 2024-25, mostly from Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab and many seeking work in sectors including hospitality, were duped by travel agents, had passports and documents seized on arrival, and were enrolled in the Russian Army and sent to war zones. Petitioners have also sought action against the recruiting agents; Bhati told the court a nodal officer had been appointed under the earlier order.

What happens next

The ministry is expected to consider the public notice, file the fresh status report on the six paid claims, and continue tracing the 77 untraced recruits. For families, the immediate path is concrete: approach their District Legal Services Authority for free legal aid on claims and DNA formalities, and work through the MEA's nodal officer rather than private agents. For the diaspora, the case is a warning that has now been repeated in court for months — overseas job offers routed through unlicensed agents, especially into conflict zones, can end with families fighting for remains and compensation years later.
